newsitem.title: USA: US investors choosier on high-yield telecom bonds.
newsitem.headline: US investors choosier on high-yield telecom bonds.

text.p: High-yield bond fund managers are still placing their bets on telecommunications and media debt amid a recent lull in issuance, but they are also now more discriminating.
Within the sector, managers said they are choosier than ever and investors have made deliberate adjustments into less speculative telecom ventures.
"The market is a little tired of looking at telecom paper," said Howard Udis, vice president and portfolio manager at SunAmerica Asset Management Co.

"It's one thing to finance a company who expects to generate cash flow in two years and a different story when it's four or five years down the road and there's technology and marketing risks," Udis noted.
Some speculative ventures will still find their way to market with higher and higher yields, he said, but investors will be leaning toward the more convincing stories -- like PanAmSat and Echostar.
"With PanAmSat and EchoStar the waiting period to cash flow positive was shorter than some of the PCS deals we have coming now," Udis said.
"Investors are looking at what the coupon is until we get to a positive event that's going to provide cash flow to the company, he said."
While some managers have grown increasingly picky, others said telecoms are overvalued and are net sellers of the debt.

Telecoms being as active as they were has led to tight spreads across much of the sector, too tight for the INVESCO Trust Co high-yield fund, said Jerry Paul, a senior vice president and portfolio manager. While sanguine on telecom credits, Paul now spies other areas like casinos for value.
"On the heels of the MFS Communications news we think some of it got ahead of itself," Paul said. "Credit-wise I like it, value-wise I don't."
At the time of the MFS/WorldCom merger announcement in late August, Paul said MFS debt was INVESCO's biggest high-yield bond holding.

John Bianchi, managing director and head of Smith Barney Inc's high-yield funds, said the promise of strong returns from telecommunication and media investments has kept his funds active in the sector as technicals eroded.

"As a manager you might find yourself underperforming for a quarter because you are overweighting telecoms as we are, but ultimately the fundamentals are very strong in terms of unit growth potential," Bianchi said.

Zero coupons were cheaper and cheaper as technicals turned against the sector, Bianchi noted, but they have begun to pay off in the absence of fresh supply. Nextel's zeros have run up four points to 61 to 61-1/2 from levels of 57 four weeks ago, for instance, and Omnipoint's 11-5/8 percent debt is up three points in three weeks to 103 bid.
Bianchi said he is now a "better seller" of high-yield based on expectations of near-term underperformance.
He still looks for the telecom credit story, though, focusing on acquisition targets and companies with market share prospects and lower capitalization needs.

More specifically, Bianchi said alternative access providers such as Teleport may not survive but some may be ripe acquisitions for veteran companies like ATT or MCI Communications Corp. At the same time, he looks to wireless providers Nextel and Omnipoint for their promise to garner market share.
INVESCO's Paul was less excited about acquisition propects for Teleport.
"I'm a skeptic on an m&a event for Teleport," he said, noting the B-rated cash pay bonds have already tightened through 300 basis point spread.

"(Teleport) is probably going to become an investment grade company someday, just not soon and to me that's a little of an evaluation stretch," Paul said. "Those are the type of things we've been selling."
